label: Frisk Without Reasonable Suspicion That the Person Was Armed and Dangerous
motion_heading: The Frisk of {client} Was Not Supported by Reasonable Suspicion That {They} {Were} Armed and Dangerous

review_conditions.display_note: You aren't sure yet what reason the officer gave for the frisk. This section was drafted anyway; get the officer's report and any body-cam footage before filing, and cut this section if the officer saw a weapon or your client said they had one.

sentences.text: An officer may frisk a person only where there is reasonable, articulable suspicion that the particular person is armed and dangerous.
The suspicion must be directed at the person frisked; suspicion of others nearby, or of the place, does not justify a frisk.
An officer's unparticularized suspicion or hunch is not enough.
The same standard applies to a passenger during a traffic stop: the officer must reasonably suspect that the passenger is armed and dangerous.
A passenger frisk during a traffic stop requires more than the passenger's mere presence in the vehicle.
General officer-safety concerns tied to the stop itself, without something specific to the passenger being frisked, do not satisfy this standard.

practice_notes: If your client was a passenger and was also asked for ID and that added time to the stop, that may raise a separate timing issue independent of the frisk itself.

A passenger has standing to challenge the stop itself and any search of their own person (Brendlin v. California, 551 U.S. 249 (2007)), but standing to challenge a search of the vehicle's contents is analyzed separately — don't assume one covers the other.
